text: I am checking whether the abstract-level hand swap misses a sharper interaction between DynaMAC’s observability assumptions and Aero Hand Open’s seven motor-encoder-only, tendon-coupled interface. Q §§2,5 says 16 joints/7 motors, only motor encoders, and sim-trained cube rotation uses a 14-D observation of channel values plus previous action; I will inspect P’s state streams, claimed generalization, and controls before proposing an experiment.

Initial read: I will test whether the distinctive junction is an observability/causal issue at handover contact, rather than a generic hand swap. Q has seven motor encoders for sixteen joints and compliant contacts (Q lines 230-281, 331-375); P defines coordination through moving end-effector/object task frames. I am checking P’s exact pose assumptions and Q’s transfer limits before committing.

Sharper candidate than a hand swap: P §4.2 (eq. gmsd) identifies an endogenous object by low variance of its pose relative to end effector and masks that stream; P §4.3 explicitly disregards gripper actions and models absolute arm end-effector poses. Q §§2,5 shows a 7-motor/16-joint tendon hand, only encoder proprioception, and demonstrated in-hand cube rotation where the object intentionally changes pose relative to the palm. Thus high relative-pose variance does not imply exogeneity: a compliant grasp can be robot-caused but nonrigid. In a handover or shared manipulation, DynaMAC’s binary exogenous/rigid-link test may retain a grasped-object stream and cause causal collapse or miscoordination. Test link detection and policy success under controlled slip/in-hand reorientation, not merely swapping grippers.

Sharper pair-specific question: does DynaMAC’s precision-based kinematic-link test identify causal attachment during a compliant, tendon-coupled grasp? P §4.2, lines 536-609 explicitly assumes that once grasped the object pose is rigidly dictated by the end-effector; near-zero relative-pose variance makes its Gaussian stream dominate, so it masks when \(M_t^{(f)}<\tau_M\) (example \(\tau_M=0.001\), about 1 mm/0.001 rad). Q §§2-3, lines 237-253, 331-375 documents underactuated fingers, silicone pads, 7 encoders for 16 joints, and contact-dependent closure. Inference: an attached object may move relative to wrist under compliance/slip, keeping \(M_t^{(f)}\) above threshold despite causal robot-to-object influence. This is a hypothesis, not a measured failure of either paper. The distinctive experiment is detector validity versus grasp compliance/contact state, not aggregate DynaMAC success on a hand swap.

Correction to my #3 and qualification to #4: P’s (M_t^{(f)}) is the spread of a learned object-frame policy stream across phase-aligned demonstrations (P §4.2 eq. gmsd), not online variance of the object/wrist transform during one rollout. In-hand motion or compliance alone does not force (M_t^{(f)}) high: a reproducible relative trajectory could remain precise and be masked. The defensible claim is a causal identification gap: neither high nor low conditional pose spread proves whether finger commands affect the object. Evaluate a range of randomized contact states/grasps and first measure detector precision/recall against controlled motor perturbation or simulator contact labels; policy failure is conditional, not established.

More direct tension with P’s bimanual claim: P §4.3 lines 730-733 says held-object pose and carrying arm pose are redundant at handover, so precise opposite-arm FK can substitute for an occluded object. P §4.1 lines 414-417 models absolute wrist/end-effector poses and explicitly sets aside gripper actions. Q §5 lines 644-649, 773-795 demonstrates in-hand cube rotation with the arm/wrist effectively fixed and no cube-pose feedback on hardware. Therefore wrist pose alone cannot determine object orientation when the hand reorients it; two physically valid hand/object states share the same arm pose yet require different receiving-hand approaches. This is a structural identifiability counterexample to P’s redundancy assumption, independent of whether GMSD happens to fire. A controlled handover varying in-hand object pose while holding wrist pose fixed would isolate it.

Ada #6 identifies the cleaner counterexample. P §4.3 (around lines 730-733) says held-object pose and carrying-arm pose are redundant, so opposite-arm FK bypasses handover occlusion. Q §4.1 gives a rank-seven (A\in\mathbb{R}^{7\times16}), §2 says only seven motor encoders, and §5 demonstrates object rotation in a stationary hand. Hence wrist pose plus motor commands/encoders need not determine object pose. Formal test: hold carrier wrist pose and motor readings in narrow bins, vary in-hand orientation/contact by controlled reseating, then estimate conditional spread (H(O\mid X_{\rm wrist},u)) from an external camera. Use an orientation-sensitive asymmetric handover target and occlude the object only at receiver inference. If distinct object poses require distinct approaches, any receiver using only the carrier FK (even plus its seven encoders) has irreducible ambiguity. Add visible-object and rigid-gripper controls. This tests P’s specific occlusion rationale; Q supplies physical mechanism and sim model. Feasibility still requires integrating Q hand plus arm and vision.

Correction to #4: Emmy #5 correctly notes P’s \(M_t^{(f)}\) is learned stream dispersion over demonstrations at a phase, not online variance in one grasp. Q’s compliant hand does not by itself imply a threshold violation. The stronger lead is #6: P’s held-object/opposite-arm pose redundancy claim has an identifiability limit under in-hand reorientation even if learned stream precision remains high. A detector-failure claim needs varied demonstrations and measured contact/causal labels.

Feasibility/claim guard: Q §3 lines 331-375 releases a MuJoCo tendon model; P §5 lines 807-813 builds DynaBench on RLBench/RLBench2. Their simulators and robot action spaces do not match, so a direct DynaBench hand swap is substantial integration. P §4.1 lines 414-417 sets gripper actions aside for exposition; I cannot infer its full implementation lacks them. The target is specifically P §4.3’s wrist-as-surrogate statement under object occlusion, not a blanket claim that DynaMAC can never handle dexterous hands. Q §5 demonstrates in-hand rotation but does not quantify object pose on hardware (lines 783-795), so magnitude of failure remains untested.

Scope correction to my #3: P §4.1 says gripper actions are disregarded *for brevity* in the pose-level exposition; it does not prove the released implementation cannot command grippers. Also Q’s physical cube pose is not logged (§6.2), so Q establishes relative motion qualitatively, not a measured conditional uncertainty or DynaMAC failure. The falsifiable target is P §4.3’s narrower FK-as-held-object-surrogate assertion under occlusion.

Proposed publishable experiment, replacing the abstract hand-swap: an occluded in-hand-reorientation handover. Write object pose as \(T_o=T_wG\), where \(T_w\) is donor wrist pose and \(G\) is the grasp-relative transform. P §4.3’s redundancy is valid if \(G\) stays effectively fixed. Q §5’s in-hand rotation proves \(G\) can change under this hand’s actuation, although its distribution and real-world magnitude are not logged. Hold donor wrist and receiver initial pose fixed; present two orientation-sensitive target orientations by rotating/reseating a marked cube in Aero Hand, then occlude the cube during receiver approach. Compare P-style opposite-wrist frame only, visible object-pose frame, and wrist plus periodic object observation/uncertainty-aware grasp-frame estimate, with a rigid-gripper and no-reorientation control. Measure conditional object-pose dispersion given wrist, contact/relative pose, grasp approach error, and success versus relative rotation and occlusion interval. If object orientation changes the safe grasp, wrist-only inputs cannot select both approaches in otherwise matched trials; if object-pose/belief input recovers, this isolates the missing state. This is a specific limitation and potential method, not a demonstrated result.

Prior-art check (queries: "robot handover in-hand object pose uncertainty occlusion dexterous hand wrist pose estimation paper"; "bimanual handover dexterous hand object pose belief occlusion proprioception paper"; "task parameterized movement primitives uncertainty object frame covariance fusion"): in-hand pose estimation under occlusion already exists, e.g. Pfanne et al., In-Hand Object Pose Tracking via Contact Feedback and GPU-Accelerated Robotic Simulation, https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.12160, and prior bimanual handover with estimated in-hand pose exists at https://doi.org/10.1080/01691864.2017.1380535. Thus do not claim pose estimation itself as novel. Plausible contribution is the specific identifiability/precision failure and uncertainty-aware object/arm stream selection in DynaMAC with Q’s encoder-only tendon hand; novelty remains to check more systematically.

Conclusion/decision: The initial generic swap has limited gain and high integration cost (Q MuJoCo vs P RLBench). The best lead is #11’s occluded in-hand-reorientation handover: P §4.3 claims donor arm FK can substitute for held-object pose, but Q §5 establishes actuation can change object pose relative to hand. This tests a specific observability assumption with a matched-state impossibility argument and visible-object/rigid-grasp controls. I judge it publication-capable only if a controlled study shows a material success gap and a practical belief/observation fix; the papers alone do not establish measured slip, conditional pose entropy, detector failure, or performance gains. I have not searched prior work, so novelty relative to the field remains unresolved. P’s learned covariance link detector is a secondary diagnostic, not the primary claim.

Information-limit guard on #11: under full occlusion and matched wrist *and* encoder/action histories, an uncertainty-aware policy cannot infer which externally reseated object orientation occurred. It may abstain, re-expose the object, or choose a robust grasp, but cannot guarantee orientation-specific success without new information. The useful method question is calibrated stream precision plus active/periodic object observation; compare to FK-only and last-seen-pose baselines. If the task can be solved by one orientation-invariant grasp, the counterexample loses force.

Cross-check of Emmy #12 prior art: arXiv:2002.12160 is by Jacky Liang et al., not Pfanne et al.; its abstract directly studies tracking in-hand object pose under occlusion during manipulation via contact feedback and simulation (https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.12160). The publisher abstract for Vezzani et al. 2017 explicitly estimates in-hand pose using vision+tactile feedback for bimanual handover (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/01691864.2017.1380535). Thus object-pose estimation and pose-aware handover are prior work; the publishable claim needs to be DynaMAC’s specific wrist-frame sufficiency/uncertainty test, not first pose-aware handover. No exhaustive novelty search completed.

Bibliography correction to #12: the 2020 ICRA paper at https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.12160 is by Jacky Liang, Ankur Handa, Karl Van Wyk, Viktor Makoviychuk, Oliver Kroemer, and Dieter Fox, not Pfanne et al. Its abstract explicitly addresses in-hand tracking under visual occlusion with contact feedback and GPU simulation. The prior-art point stands; Q lacks that contact feedback.

Agree with Emmy #14: in exactly matched wrist/encoder/action histories with complete occlusion, no estimator can recover the correct object orientation. Revise #11’s remedy: uncertainty-aware policy must represent ambiguity and obtain new information (re-expose/object view or active probing) or take a grasp robust to both orientations; it cannot infer a hidden externally reseated pose from Q’s seven encoders alone. Use last-seen-pose and active-view baselines, and make the task orientation-sensitive while verifying no single invariant grasp succeeds.

My final assessment: replace abstract scan’s generic two-hand DynaBench swap with Ada #11’s matched-state, orientation-sensitive handover. P §4.3’s donor-FK surrogate presumes stable (G=T_w^{-1}T_o); Q §§2,5 supplies an encoder-only tendon hand capable of changing (G) by in-hand rotation. The decisive first result is empirical (p(G\mid T_w,u_{0:t})) and receiver success under occlusion, with matched wrist/encoder histories, rigid-grasp and visible-object controls. The causal/precision detector from P §4.2 is secondary because its spread is across demonstrations and may or may not flag the mode. A method result would calibrate object-pose belief into P’s stream precision or seek a view when ambiguous; no policy can recover orientation under truly indistinguishable, fully occluded states. Unresolved: measurable pose spread on real Q hardware (cube pose unlogged in Q), contact-model fidelity, integration burden, whether orientation-invariant grasps erase the effect, and field novelty beyond known pose trackers/handover work (Liang et al. 2020; Vezzani et al. 2017). Publication potential is conditional on a material controlled failure plus recovery.
